newsitem.title: UK: Underdog Major fights to avoid British polls defeat.
newsitem.headline: Underdog Major fights to avoid British polls defeat.

text.p: Despite polls pointing to a crushing defeat for his ruling Conservative Party, Prime Minister John Major said on Wednesday he had not given up hope of victory in Thursday's British election.
As party leaders set out to court the country's 44 million voters in the last 24 hours of campaigning, Major said: "I don't share the opinion that we're going to lose tomorrow.
"I think this election is there to be won. There are huge numbers of people who are undecided," Major told BBC radio.
Opposition leader Tony Blair, whose Labour Party last won an election in 1974, also brushed aside opinion polls showing his party about 20 points ahead and heading for a landslide.
Blair, who has termed himself the "eternal warrior against complacency", said he would not let up until polling booths closed on Thursday evening (2100 GMT).

"We will not stop trying to persuade people to put their trust in Labour. Between now and when the polls close tomorrow night we will strive for every vote, in every corner of the country," he told an eve-of-poll news conference.
"Because this election is not going to be decided by opinion polls. It is not going to be resolved by pundits. It is in the hands of the British people."
Labour's lead has been steady for two years and has held up since Major called the election on March 17, hoping to wear Labour down with the longest campaign for more than 80 years.

No party has come back from such a poll deficit to win an election. Major pulled off a surprise win almost single-handedly in 1992 but a Conservative victory on Thursday would arguably be the biggest electoral sensation since 1945, when voters threw out victorious war-time prime minister Winston Churchill in a Labour landslide.

This time Labour needs a vote swing of 4.3 percent from the Conservatives over 1992 figures to win an overall majority and end 18 years of Conservative rule - the longest unbroken stretch of the 20th century.

The 20-point lead shown by current polls would give Labour a majority of around 200 seats. But no one is expecting that size of victory and the overall picture is complicated by Britain's first-past-the-post electoral system.
Blair has revitalised Labour since becoming leader in July 1994 by dragging it from the left to the political centreground.

Blair's radical modernisation of his party, which has involved ditching its traditional socialist dogma and promising tight control of public spending and pragmatic social policies, also seemed to be working its spell in financial markets.

Blue chip shares reached a new high in early trading on Wednesday while sterling remained firm on foreign exchange markets. In the past, the spectre of a Labour landslide would have sent sterling plunging and share prices through the floor.

During a radio phone-in on Wednesday, Major came in for hostile questioning even from his own supporters, one of whom accused him of being "complacent" and of having lost the election. But he continued to warn of the economic cost of a Labour victory.

Major said the economy was in the best shape "for generations". He added: "I think the fundamental reason people will pause before taking the risk of changing to the Labour Party is that there is so much at risk at the moment," he said.
Blair repeated his stock promise that Labour's limited but specific commitments, especially in education and health, would make a difference to ordinary voters.
"If people think that Britain could be better they should vote for a new and modern Labour Party that can deliver," Blair told a news conference.
Support for the minority Liberal Democrats is holding firm at around 15 percent compared to Labour's 50 and the Conservatives 30 percent.

The Liberal Democrats could hold the balance of power if neither Labour nor the Conservatives gain a majority. They are expected to support Labour in such a scenario, with radical reform of the voting system the price for their cooperation.
